content: Active immunization involves the introduction of an actual microbe into a person’s body. The individual’s immune system responds by producing antibodies, which are then stored permanently for future defense against the same microbe. Natural active immunization occurs when a person, who has not previously encountered a specific microbe and therefore lacks pre-existing antibodies, is exposed to the untreated microbe. In this case, the immune system eventually generates antibodies to combat the microbe. However, this process is slow, and if the microbe is particularly virulent or deadly, the immune system may not produce antibodies quickly enough to prevent severe illness or death. Artificial active immunization, on the other hand, involves the deliberate introduction of the microbe into the person’s body before they are naturally exposed to it. In this method, the microbe is treated to ensure it does not cause harm to the individual. Depending on the disease, this approach can utilize live but weakened microbes, inactivated (dead) microbes, specific components of the microbe, or toxins produced by the microbe that have been rendered harmless.
